attribute_differences.csv_raw: Prentice et al. (2003) present evidence from a trench at the Rio Licey along the central Septentrtional fault in the Cibao Valley. The fault is not expressed at the surface, but subsurface units record minor faulting and folding. Radiocarbon samples indicate the earthquake is constraint to before A.D. 1440-1640 and after A.D. 780-1220. The penultimate event is recorded by offset stratigraphy that dates to A.D. 30-240 which may represent the maximum age of event. A third older event may be recorded that dates to <4850-5380 yr BP and >2890-3360 yr BP). A flight of offset fluvial terrace risers records left-lateral movement and fault scarps with opposite facing directions and heights of 3-8 m. Prentice et al. (2003) estimate a maximum left-lateral offset of 60 m on the youngest terrace, which dates to 5380-4850 yr BP, yielding a maximum slip rate of 11-12 mm/yr,

attribute_differences.csv_raw: Piety et al. (2018) present lidar and air-photo mapping and paleoseismic data from a trench site (TM1) along the Salinas fault on a 2-m-high south-facing scarp. Evidence of latest Pleistocene and possibly Holocene earthquake ruptures based on 1) juxtaposed debris flow and fluvial units, 2) near-vertical faults and fractures with consistent upward termination points, and 3) changes in carbonate fabric on footwall side of fault. They interpret two earthquake ruptures on the Salinas fault between ~2 and 10 ka based on OSL, or possibly at 8–14 ka and >14 ka based on conflicting C14 ages. Recurrence on the Salinas may be ~4 kyr, but estimate is limited by small sample size and conflicting geochronologic ages. Calcium carbonate fabric in the trench also suggests an older event(s), with OSL ages constraining the timing of deformation  before 16-21 ka.

attribute_differences.csv_raw: Feuillet et al. (2010) interpret bathymetry and geophysical data along the Bouillante-Montserrat fault system between Montserrat and Guadelupe. Using K-Ar ages of older volcanic centers on Guadelupe (from Sampers et al., 2007) and their interpreted left-lateral displacements from the active volcanic centers, the authors estimate a left-lateral slip rate of ~5 mm/yr over the last 800 ka. Uncertainties in the ages of the Sans-Toucher volcanic center, the authors interpret the slip rate may vary by a factor of 2.

attribute_differences.csv_raw: Southwest Puerto Rico polygon

Zachariasen and von Hildebrante-Andrade (2005) excavated 2 paleoseismic trenches at the Escuela site across the interpreted location of the Cerro Goden fault. No fault was exposed in trench Escuela 1, but the trench did reveal a north-facing buried scarp. Trench Escuela 2 was excavated across a fault identified in seismic reflection data. The trench revealed a juxtaposition of fluvial channel and overbank deposits with red clays with gravel lenses that coincided with the updip projection of the fault interpreted on the seismic reflection data. The authors interpret that the relationship is most likely explained by a buttress unconformity.

attribute_differences.csv_raw: Piety et al. (2018) present lidar and air-photo mapping and paleoseismic data from a trench site (TC1) along the Great Southern Puerto Rico fault zone (GSPRFZ) on a 0.7-m-high scarp. Two ruptures on the GSPRFZ likely occurred during the latest Pleistocene and possibly Holocene, although no radiometric ages were reported. Soils  are interpreted to be consistent with trench TM1 soils and thus latest Pleistocene and possibly Holocene in age. The penultimate event produced >1m of vertical separation, whereas MRE had little-to-no vertical expression, interpreted to be mostly lateral.
